messages.subject: Same model, different abundance
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I'm working with “dsm” package in R to obtain abundance estimates of a local dolphin population.

Over my study area I have applied two grids with different cell size (4 or 8 nautical miles), to obtain predictive maps of different resolution. The data of each variable have been adjusted to the cell size of each grid to fit different models. When fitting the models, both models selected the same variables (all of them statistically significant), but the abundance estimates were really different. The results of each model were:

8 miles grid model:

Abundance: 84272

DE: 15.3%

R2: 0.03

GCV: 3.97

4 miles grid model:

Abundance: 44360

DE: 16.4%

R2: 0.04

GCV: 5.84

What explains this huge difference?
If you have to choose a model, which one would you choose? Considering that both model cannot be compared, because for fitting them I have used “different data” (the same data, but adjusted to each cell size).
Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Same model, different abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paula, hi listfolk,

I don't think there is an easy answer to your question, but perhaps the
below is useful:

If (as a simplistic example) you had 25 x 1km^2 cells arranged in a 5x5
grid, but some cells had vastly different values (as can happen for say,
high resolution, remotely-sensed sea surface temperature or chlorophyll)
but then estimated abundance at the 5km^2 grid size too, you might
expect rather different things to happen for the model and predictions.

Thinking about abundance estimates (but not changing the data in the
model): there might be a couple values of SST that correspond to a very
small predicted abundance in the model. At 1km^2 cells, these show up
and contribute only a very small value to the abundance. But when the
cell values are averaged over the 5km^2, the larger cell has an SST
value that corresponds to larger predicted values in the model.

Similar arguments hold for the model fitting process too -- taking lower
resolution data by averaging smaller cells leads to a loss of
information that would then lead to a different model (or rather,
different shapes of the smooths in the model) being selected. This loss
of information may not necessarily be bad: it's possible that the
variable is too noisy and the estimated smooth relationship is actually
too wiggly (i.e. the model has overfitted).

Unfortunately the answer to "which would you choose" is highly
context-dependent. Not only does it depend on the scale of the study and
the taxon involved, but also it's dependent on what you want your
predictions to mean too (for example when averaging over a temporally
varying covariate such as SST or chlorophyll). Finally, the kind of
average that you take can have an influence on the resulting model and
predictions too.

It's worth noting that the models have the same form, but are different
in the sense that they use different data and hence have different
parameter estimates.

I'd recommend looking into the literature for more information on this
and how you might test to see which model is preferable. A starting
point that might be useful is this (open access) paper:

Redfern, J. V., Barlow, J., Ballance, L. T., Gerrodette, T., & Becker,
E. A. (2008). Absence of scale dependence in dolphin–habitat models for
the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 363,
1–14. http://doi.org/10.3354/meps07495

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

PS. I note you're comparing GCV scores here. In our 2013 paper, we
recommend against using GCV for smoothness selection in DSMs as they
tend to have less useful theoretical properties (and in my experience,
can lead to rather odd models). I'd recommend setting method="REML" in
your dsm call to try to use REML for smoothness selection. More details
are available in:

Miller, DL, ML Burt, EA Rexstad and L Thomas (2013). Spatial models for
distance sampling data: recent developments and future directions.
Methods in Ecology and Evolution.
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract
(Also open access)

and an example analysis at:
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/mexico-analysis.html

messages.body_plain:
Chapter 8 (Conventional Distance Sampling) of the Users Guide to Program Distance says:

Exporting Plots or Plot Data
To transfer a high-resolution plot, make sure the plot is showing and then click
on the Copy to Clipboard button on the main toolbar, or choose the Analysis
– Results menu button Copy Plot to Clipboard. You can only paste the plot
itself into applications that are designed to take picture objects, such as word
processors and spreadsheets. In your application, choose Paste Special, and
then choose the option “Picture” from the list of formats that appears (you can
also choose “Device Independent Bitmap”, but you will end up with a much
larger file).
Alternatively, you can paste the data that was used to generate the plot file into,
say, a spreadsheet and then regenerate the file yourself. This has the advantage
that you can then change the format of the plot. To do this, in your application,
choose Paste, or choose Paste Special and then the “Unformatted Text”
option.

messages.body_plain:
Hi
Currently, I am analyzing data from lineal distance sampling for Tamarin Saguinus leucopus. I have fitted models with six combinations of detection functions and expansion series: uniform/simple polynomial, uniform/cosine, half-normal/cosine, half-normal/hermite polynomial, hazard-rate/cosine, and hazard-rate/simple polynomial.
Althought the models have run without problems, the results for models with half-normal function and cosine and hermite polynomial series are the same. Similar situation is observed with hazard rate function and cosine and simple polynomial series.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Problems with series adjustment
messages.body_plain:
Camilo

Nothing wrong (that I can see) with what you have done.  When you ask Distance to fit models with a "key" function and "adjustment", Distance first fits the key function without any adjustment terms. It then fits a model with an adjustment term added; AIC model selection takes place to learn whether the adjustment term improved the model performance.  If no improvement took place, fitting stops and the preferred model (with no adjustment terms) is returned.

This is the situation you show, in which you tried two types of adjustment series for the hazard rate key function, and in both cases, a model with no adjustment terms was preferred.  You can deduce this by looking at the number of parameters in the fitted model.  The hazard key function has 2 parameters; if there were adjustment terms, those would be additional parameters to estimate.  Both your hazard rate models show 2 estimated parameters, meaning no adjustment terms were selected.  A hazard rate model with 0 simple polynomial adjustments is EXACTLY THE SAME MODEL as a hazard rate model with 0 cosine adjustment terms.

Same story applied to your half normal key function.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Eric

Thank you for your very clear and helpful answer.

Now I understand what was the "wrong" with my models. I am going to fit additional models with an adjustment term to test whether it improves the models performance.

I would want to make you an additional question about the goodness fit tests.

I am using Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test because distance data are continuous (I am not using grouped data in distance intervals). The K-S test for my best fitted model reached a p value of 0.0863 (D_n=0.0714). From this result I understand that there is no evidence of lack of fit for model. Likewise, the visual inspection of QQ plot graphic shows low discrepancy between observed distances and the distribution of predicted distances.

Considering that p value in K-S test is near to 0.05, it is necessary fitting models with data grouped in intervals distance and testing if the goodness fit for X2 test could be better than K-S test.

Thanks a lot!!!

Camilo Sánchez

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Problems with series adjustment
messages.body_plain:
Camilo

For absolute measures of model fit (GOF tests, as opposed to relative measures of fit using AIC), the threshhold is what you accept as the Type I error rate.  If the P-value on your KS test exceed 0.05 (or whatever you have used as alpha), then you are making inference with a model that fits the data.

I do not advocate messing about with adjustments of cut points to "improve the fit" of chi-square tests.

messages.subject_clean: Difference between MCDS and MRDS engines for single platform estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been working on a mark-recapture estimate, io, point independence. My first step is generally to work out the combined platform estimate using the MCDS engine, as it is a bit more convenient to use and gives nicer output than the MRDS engine. I then specify the same MCDS model in the MRDS engine and proceed to develop the mark-recapture model.

I have noticed that the combined platform estimates developed with the MCDS engine differ substantially from those developed with the MRDS engine, specifying method "ds-single observer". Now, I realize that the manual says that they will differ slightly, but in this case the MRDS single platform estimate is 12% higher than the equivalent MCDS estimate. Also the CV's are substantially different.

I thought this might be a result of size bias correction of cluster size, which is not applied in the MRDS model, but that is not the case as it has little effect. I also was not sure if MRDS estimated cluster size at the global or stratum level, but it appears to do so at the stratum level, which is the same as I am doing in the MCDS model.

The 12% difference actually exceeds the MR correction, so it is not unsubstantial. I don't understand the reason for the difference, or which estimate is "correct".

My inclination is to apply the p(0) developed with MRDS to the combined platform estimate from the MCDS estimate, but I am not sure that this is the correct approach and would be more comfortable if I knew what the source of the discrepancy is.

Any help would be appreciated.

Regards,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel, hi listfolk,

As you rightly state, there are often minor differences in the parameter
estimates for the detection functions estimated by the MCDS and MRDS
engines. These are usually down to differences in the optimisation
algorithm in these two approaches.

Just to check: when you analyse the combined data with the MCDS engine
have you ensured that only one observer's data? It's worth checking that
the number of observations is the same for both, and the difference is
not just down to having double the observers and double the observations.

For a while it was the case that the MCDS engine's estimates were better
than those from the MRDS engine, but we're now finding more cases and
improving the MRDS code such that the MRDS engine is out-performing the
MCDS engine (in likelihood terms). This seems (from personal experience)
highly dependent on the data set.

I'd recommend checking the likelihood that comes out of both models and
see which has the better value -- this might provide some more
information on what's going on (and which engine is to "blame").

An additional related issue may be that for an MRDS model we have two
likelihood components: one for the detection function and one for the
detection function at zero distance. The MRDS engine will fit each
separately, then do a combined optimisation on both at the end to ensure
that the best parameters have been found. So comparing an MCDS engine
model and just the detection function part of an MRDS engine model, you
might find differences. (Though I understand that's not what you mean here.)

Please feel free to send me your results/code off-list and I'll be happy
to take a look.

cheers,
--dave

Dear Eric, Philippe and all list-users,

Sorry for a late reply, but I had to manage other projects since last time.

With Eric help, I have been able to compute the detection probability for hares using the half-normal key function with hermite polynomial and also covariates (years and area).

Here is the code I used and the final plot for year 2006 :
final$ddf$par
# Intercept[1]          CovYear2007[2]          CovYear2008[3]          CovYear2009[4]          CovYear2010[5]
# 5.163597494            -0.077848472            -0.003582774            -0.048619934            -0.103227843
# CovYear2011[6]        CovYear2012[7]          CovYear2013[8]     zoneBARROIS.Nord.A5[9]  zoneSARCE.plaine.Seine[10]
# -0.118052539             0.089956855             0.063322206             0.048347985             0.050961822
# zoneSARCE.plateau.côtes[11]       herm[12]
# -0.034803549                  0.051477479
# half-normal + hermite polynomial (order 4) + Covyear + Zone
g.herm.cov <- function(y,param,w,an07,an08,an09,an10,an11,an12,an13,barN,sarPla,sarCo){
  param <- unname(param)
  nu      <- param[1] + an07*param[2] + an08*param[3] + an09*param[4] + an10*param[5] + an11*param[6] + an12*param[7] + an13*param[8] + barN*param[9] + sarPla*param[10] + sarCo*param[11]
  sigma   <- exp(nu)
  x       <- y/w
  key     <- exp(-y^2/(2*sigma^2))
  key0    <- exp(-(0)^2/(2*sigma^2))
  serie   <- 1+exp(param[12]*(x^4-6*x^2+3))  # following Distance 7.0 User's manual p.101, Hermite polynomial of order 4 is : x^4-6*x^2+3
  serie0  <- 1+exp(param[12]*(0^4-6*0^2+3))
  pdet    <- key*(1+serie)/(key0*(1+serie0))
  return(pdet)
}
dist <- seq(0,600,0.5)
Barrois.Sud  <- g.herm.cov(dist,final$ddf$par,final$ddf$ds$aux$width,an07=0,an08=0,an09=0,an10=0,an11=0,an12=0,an13=0,barN=0,sarPla=0,sarCo=0)
Barrois.nord <- g.herm.cov(dist,final$ddf$par,final$ddf$ds$aux$width,an07=0,an08=0,an09=0,an10=0,an11=0,an12=0,an13=0,barN=1,sarPla=0,sarCo=0)
Sarce.Plaine <- g.herm.cov(dist,final$ddf$par,final$ddf$ds$aux$width,an07=0,an08=0,an09=0,an10=0,an11=0,an12=0,an13=0,barN=0,sarPla=1,sarCo=0)
sarce.Cotes  <- g.herm.cov(dist,final$ddf$par,final$ddf$ds$aux$width,an07=0,an08=0,an09=0,an10=0,an11=0,an12=0,an13=0,barN=0,sarPla=0,sarCo=1)

plot(dist,Barrois.Sud,type="n",main = "Hares detection in 2006 \n HalfNorm + Herm^4",
     ylab="Detection probability",xlab = "Distance")
lines(dist,Barrois.Sud,type="l",col="red",lty=3,lwd=2)
lines(dist,Barrois.nord,col="orange",lty=1,lwd=2)
lines(dist,Sarce.Plaine,col="blue",lty=3,lwd=2)
lines(dist,sarce.Cotes,col="green",lty=1,lwd=2)
legend("topright",legend = c("Barrois Sud","Barrois Nord","Sarce Plaine","Sarce Côtes"),
       col=c("red","orange","blue","green"),lty = c(3,1,3,1),lwd = 2, title = "Zone")

lines(dist,sarce.Cotes,col="green",lty=1,lwd=2)
legend("topright",legend = c("Barrois Sud","Barrois Nord","Sarce Plaine","Sarce Côtes"),
       col=c("red","orange","blue","green"),lty = c(3,1,3,1),lwd = 2, title = "Zone")

messages.subject: Loosely grouped target species
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance Samplers

A question please on how to allocate loosely grouped animals to distance classes.

Some animal species, for example kangaroos and wild horses, roam in loose clusters rather than in tightly grouped mobs. When sighting such loosely grouped animals from an aircraft, what is the preferred approach when members of a group span a number of distance classes?

If I came across say 7 animals, 2 in the 0-30m distance class, 4 in the 30-80m, and 1 in the 80-150m, should I record sighting 3 groups in their respective distance classes, with group sizes of 2, 4 and 1, or should I record just the single group, and assign all 7 animals to the 30-80m bin?

Is one approach the more preferred, while the other will lead to statistical damnation?

Many thanks for your insights, Terry

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Loosely grouped target species
messages.body_plain:
Terry, I would collect the data in such a way that both options are available.  You can then check whether it makes much difference.  I would not expect it to.  The methods in Distance are very robust to non-independence, so I would prefer the option where you split the group between the distance intervals.  However, the model selection tools (goodness-of-fit, AIC) tend to suggest over-fitting in this circumstance.  You could select the detection function on an analysis with all animals in a group assigned to one distance interval, corresponding to the group centre, and then fit only that model (fixing the number of adjustment terms to the value obtained in that analysis) to the data where animals are split between intervals.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: rock ptarmigan surveys multiple observers
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance samplers,

We are studying the techniques of estimation of densities for rock ptarmigan in the Pyrenees.
We work from historical surveys of the species, using the point count methode. For security reasons and for augment the precision of the bird localizations, the observers are distributed forming a “mesh” approx. 250m between two observers, all observers are independents (no communication between observers during the survey). This technique allows a better localization of the singing bird, when two or sometimes three observers detect the same bird. It is very difficult to see the bird, so we mapped the approximate position of the calling bird on a topographic map (1: 25,000 scale). We then measured the distance from observer to the position of each bird using a GIS programe.
Currently we analyze this data’s with CDS, and when 2 or 3 observers detect the same bird we only conserve the shortest observation distance. This is a false good solution because we lose a part of the information.
We have read the bibliography, but we have not found a similar case. We thought the MCDS is may be a solution but this technique is only use for line transects…
The question we have, is how we can introduce this data’s (one bird detected for 1, 2 or 3 observers) on Distance sampling, and how should we analyze these data?

Thank you very much,
Cordially,

Gaël ALEIX

Gaël, if a given bird is recorded by three observers, you should include it three times, one for each point it was detected from.  Multiple-recording of the same bird from different points is discussed in detail in

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of aleix mata gaël
Sent: 25 February 2016 13:28
To: distance-sampling
Subject: [distance-sampling] rock ptarmigan surveys multiple observers

Dear Distance samplers,

We are studying the techniques of estimation of densities for rock ptarmigan in the Pyrenees.
We work from historical surveys of the species, using the point count methode. For security reasons and for augment the precision of the bird localizations, the observers are distributed forming a “mesh” approx. 250m between two observers, all observers are independents (no communication between observers during the survey). This technique allows a better localization of the singing bird, when two or sometimes three observers detect the same bird. It is very difficult to see the bird, so we mapped the approximate position of the calling bird on a topographic map (1: 25,000 scale). We then measured the distance from observer to the position of each bird using a GIS programe.
Currently we analyze this data’s with CDS, and when 2 or 3 observers detect the same bird we only conserve the shortest observation distance. This is a false good solution because we lose a part of the information.
We have read the bibliography, but we have not found a similar case. We thought the MCDS is may be a solution but this technique is only use for line transects…
The question we have, is how we can introduce this data’s (one bird detected for 1, 2 or 3 observers) on Distance sampling, and how should we analyze these data?

Thank you very much,
Cordially,

Gaël ALEIX

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Warning translation CDS method
messages.body_plain:
Gilles

I suspect that warning is arising when you are trying to fit a hazard rate model...  That family of detection functions has 2 parameters sigma and beta. Even if fitting a half-normal detection function, with a single parameter, you have only 3 "points of support" from the bins into which you combined your detection distances. If in addition to that, you are allowing adjustment terms (which add additional parameters to be estimated), you will soon have as many parameters in your detection function model as you have points of support (3 bins for your detection distances).  That will leave little information in the data with which to assess the goodness of fit of your model to your data.

In general, it is unwise to use many parameters (relative to your data support).
